messages.author: 5d56b85b4ef83da0
messages.subject: Multiple sightings on a point
parts:
Hi, I have recently imported data from a point survey into Distance 4.1
and I having a few problems with getting feasible results in the analysis
stage. I was hoping that someone out there could help me answer some of the
following questions:

1. One of our areas had 694 points that we stopped at. Of those, 40
points had sightings,
some with more than one animal observed. Often these animals were
observed at different
locations. How do you therefore import the data so that you have the
information for
more than one animal on one survey point? At the moment we are having to
import multiple
sightings on different points.

2. When it we have run the analyses of any information we have imported
there are a few areas
that are causing a bit of confusion for us. At the top of the Detection
Fct/Global//Model Fitting
page it lists :
we are interpreting the data as follows:

Effort is the number of times each point was visited which is each point
was visited once.

The number of samples is causing confusion for us as there are 40 points
where we observed
animals. What are we doing wrong here or is this right?
Width is the effective radial distance of the points.

Number of observations is equal to the number of points that we stopped
at.

If some of the above is wrong please could you help.

I apologise for the long winded nature of this e-mail but I thought it best
to try and explain our problems in detail.

I thank anyone who can help.

Cheers.

Dave Tosh.
Queens University Belfast.

messages.author: 4b4a7b00c1dd09c7
messages.subject: Re: Multiple sightings on a point
parts:
Hi David,

Tiago Marques wrote the following; I'm cc'ing it to the list so it's in the
archives in case anyone else gets in the same pickle. I assume you've read the
online manual, particularly Chapter 4 on Data in Distance, which has an example
similar to Tiago's below.

Cheers,

- Len

On Tue, 18 May 2004 17:29:23 +0100, Tiago Andre Lamas Oliveira Marques
<tama...@fc.ul.pt> wrote:

> >Hi David,

> >It's easier to answer your question by first explaining the bit of output you
ask about.

>> >> Effort : 1.000000
>> >> # samples : 1
>> >> Width : 80.00000
>> >> # observations: 694

>> > > Effort is the number of times each point was visited which is each point
>> >>was visited once.

> >Effort is the total effort. If you have points, and each point was done only
once, should be the same as #samples. If you had say, 6 points, but one had been
done twice, Effort would be 7. If each point had been done twice, Effort would
be 12.

>> >>The number of samples is causing confusion for us as there are 40 points
>> >>where we observed
>> >> animals. What are we doing wrong here or is this right?

> >Somehow the software is interpreting that you only have a point, not the 694!
The number of samples should be the number of points in your survey area
(irrespectively of having detected animals on them or not).

>> >> Width is the effective radial distance of the points.

> >Width is the largest distance used in the analysis. That could be either your
largest detection distance or (if you use a truncation distance) the truncation
distance.

>> >> Number of observations is equal to the number of points that we stopped
>> >>at.

> >The number of observations should be the number of detections, not 694. Part of
the problem might be that if you have a point with no observations, you should
have a line with no distance in it. If you put a 0, the software assumes that
you have a distance of 0, not that you have no distance at all. However, this
alone would not explain your results, as if you have at least one point with
more than one sighting, and you say you do, the number of observations would be
higher that 694.

> >Maybe it's simpler to look at an example. Let's assume you had a study area,
with 10ha, and that you had 2 strata (in your case, there is probably no need
for strata information), with 3 points in each, and that in the strata A (3 ha)
you had 3 birds in the second point (but none in point 1 or 3), and in strata B
(7 ha) you had one bird in point 1 and 2, and 2 birds in point 3. A data file
(in a txt file, which you could then import to Distance) would look like this

> >Area Statum STRArea Point Effort Observation
> >10 StrA 3 1 1
> >10 StrA 3 2 1 2.3
> >10 StrA 3 2 1 0
> >10 StrA 3 2 1 4.5
> >10 StrA 3 3 1
> >10 StrB 7 1 1 3.1
> >10 StrB 7 2 1 2.3
> >10 StrB 7 3 1 4.2
> >10 StrB 7 3 1 2.1

> >(notice that you have a 0 distance in point 2, stratum A, and 2 points with no
detection in strata A)

> >In this case, the output from distance (assuming no truncation) would be

> > Effort : 6.000000
> > # samples : 6
> > Width : 4.5
> > # observations: 7

> >So, bottom line, you need (at least) 1 line for each point, and if more than
one animal is detected at 1 point, you need one line for each detected animal.
Let me know if you need more help on this.

> >Cheers,

> >Tiago
